what: Eagle Materials makes basic construction materials. It produces cement, concrete and aggregates sold regionally, and gypsum wallboard and the recycled paperboard used to face it, sold to homebuilders and commercial contractors across the United States.
customers: Homebuilders, commercial construction contractors, highway and infrastructure contractors, and building materials distributors, mostly in the central and southern United States.
money: Cement, concrete and aggregates sold within trucking distance of each plant.
moat: Cement is expensive to transport relative to its value, so each plant has a natural local market that distant competitors cannot economically serve. New cement plants are almost never permitted in the United States because of the emissions and the planning difficulty, which makes existing capacity a protected asset. Eagle also owns the paperboard that faces its own wallboard, which few competitors do.
risks: Free cash flow of $155.5M against $376.7M of net income is a large gap, because cement plants require continuous heavy capital investment.
Revenue has been flat at about $2.3B for three years, as housing construction slowed.
Wallboard demand tracks housing starts closely, and housing starts have been weak.
Debt of $1.8B against $297.9M of cash has risen as the company has bought back stock.
Ten analysts average a $194.10 target, about 12% above the current price.
opportunities: Last year’s net margin was 18.4%, which is exceptional for building materials and reflects the local monopoly economics of cement.
The shares trade at about 14.4 times earnings and 10.2 times EV/EBITDA.
New cement capacity is almost impossible to permit in the United States, which protects existing plants permanently.
Infrastructure spending supports cement demand independently of housing.
Owning the paperboard that faces its own wallboard is a vertical integration advantage few competitors have.
watch: Cement volumes and pricing by region, separately from wallboard. Cement is the protected local-monopoly business and wallboard is the housing-cycle business, and they behave differently.
view: Cement is one of the best businesses in industrial America for a reason that has nothing to do with the product: it is too heavy to ship far. Transporting cement more than a few hundred kilometres costs more than the cement is worth, so every plant has a natural local market that distant competitors cannot economically enter. Combine that with the fact that new cement plants are almost never permitted in the United States — the emissions and the planning process make it practically impossible — and you have a set of local monopolies protected by physics and bureaucracy together.

That is what an 18.4% net margin on building materials means. It is not operational excellence; it is pricing power in markets where the alternative supplier is too far away to matter. Infrastructure spending supports this demand independently of housing, which gives the heavy materials half a different and steadier driver.

The wallboard half is a different business and should be analysed separately. Gypsum wallboard tracks housing starts almost directly, and housing starts have been weak as mortgage rates kept buyers and sellers in place. Eagle does have a genuine advantage here — it owns the recycled paperboard that faces its own wallboard, which few competitors do, giving it control over a key input cost — but no integration advantage overcomes a cycle.

At 14.4 times earnings and 10.2 times EV/EBITDA with revenue flat at $2.3 billion for three years, you are paying a modest multiple for protected assets in a weak part of the cycle. The gap between $377 million of net income and $156 million of free cash flow deserves attention: cement plants consume heavy, continuous capital investment, and that is a permanent feature rather than a timing issue. This is a good business at a reasonable price waiting for housing, and cement volumes and pricing by region are where the quality actually shows.
bull: Housing recovers while infrastructure spending supports cement, and protected local-monopoly plants that nobody can permit again earn 18% margins through the cycle.
bear: Housing stays frozen for years, wallboard volumes fall, and heavy ongoing plant capital spending keeps free cash flow well below reported earnings.
